title: Deterministic Verification and a Single‑Repair Guardrail for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: a Paired, Shared‑Candidate Study
abstract: We report a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment that measured the verifier-confirmed effect of inserting a deterministic validator plus up to one automated repair (a guarded generate–verify–repair pipeline) on the same LLM-generated configuration candidate. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics we generated one initial candidate per natural-language intent (gpt-5-mini) for N=250 paired intents and applied a deterministic network validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) with ≤1 automated repair on the guarded branch. Results: baseline verifier-pass 249/250 (99.6%), guarded verifier-pass 250/250 (100.0%); paired difference = +0.4 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp], exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. One discordant pair was corrected by the single permitted repair. The preregistered design (study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1) and the repaired preregistration artifact (SHA-256 = 7a984dbf7265c9a774eaf95c6c930dcf5f1e8845088bbc0e0855e3b4f1000ede) are archived; the master-prompt provenance file used to initiate the autonomous run is provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). We explicitly state shared_initial_candidate semantics, reconcile preregistered scope with executed confirmatory estimand, explain provider-call accounting, and discuss limits on external validity.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are actively explored to convert operator intent into concrete network configurations, but stochastic generation raises operational correctness and safety concerns. Prior work proposes interposing deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–verify–repair, GVR) to detect and correct mechanically checkable defects [1–6]. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to quantify the incremental verifier-confirmed benefit of deterministic validation plus a single automated repair versus accepting the identical raw LLM candidate. The paper's contributions are: (1) a preregistered, artifact-backed paired evaluation using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator on N=250 intent pairs; (2) a strict shared_initial_candidate execution and exact paired inference that isolates validator+repair effects; and (3) an evidence-grounded near-null primary result with explicit reconciliation of preregistration, execution accounting, and statistical interpretation.
sections.related_work: Work applying LLMs to intent→configuration and NetOps automation shows that LLMs can produce usable draft configurations but often require verification or human oversight [7–12]. Architectures that place deterministic checkers and repair loops between stochastic generators and acceptance have been proposed and shown to reduce mechanically verifiable defects in code and configuration domains [2,3,5]. Mature deterministic network analyzers and formal methods (Batfish, header-space, model checking) provide mechanistic validators in prior research [8,13–15]. Security analyses demonstrate prompt-injection threats to LLM pipelines and motivate verifier/filter layers [16]. This study builds on these threads by executing a sealed, preregistered, shared-candidate comparison that isolates the validator+repair effect on existing candidates.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: The study was preregistered as study-cand-2026-LLM-verifier-sim2real-v1 and the repaired preregistration artifact (SHA-256 = 7a984dbf7...) was fixed prior to execution. That preregistration explicitly declared generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial candidate per intent shared across paired episodes) and specified the primary estimand as paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration also enumerated partitions (emulation/synthetic, community, production-like) but the confirmatory contract and task_count = 250 applied to the emulation/synthetic partition only; community and production-like partitions were listed as exploratory and were not executed in the confirmatory run. Design and execution: A deterministic task generator produced N_pairs = 250 constrained intent tasks. For each intent we generated a single shared initial response using the declared model gpt-5-mini; that same initial candidate was used for two episodes: baseline (accepted as-is; no repair) and guarded (deterministic validator run; if validator failed, a single automated repair attempt was permitted). Tooling: declared model gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); deterministic validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5; task generator deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Execution contract limited model calls to the preregistered maximum_model_calls = 500 and allowed ≤1 repair call per episode. Scoring and inference: the validator returned a boolean verifier_pass per episode; the primary test was exact McNemar two-sided on the paired contingency table; the 95% CI used the preregistered paired bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exclusions: preregistered exclusion rules (parser-blocking syntax, credential tokens, private-address blocks) were applied; no exclusion occurred. All prompts, model outputs, validator traces, and repair traces were recorded immutably in the archived evidence bundle.
sections.results: Execution accounting and provider-call reconciliation: planned_episode_count = 500 (250 pairs × 2 episodes); completed_episode_count = 500; model_calls_used = 251 (250 shared initial generations + 1 repair call). The execution manifest stage_counts (shared_initial_generation = 250; repair = 1) and provider audit fields reflect the shared_initial_candidate semantics rather than independent first-pass generations per condition; the single repair call explains the model_calls_used total. Primary outcome: complete_pair_count = 250; baseline_success_count = 249 (0.996); guarded_success_count = 250 (1.0). Paired contingency (guarded, baseline): n11 = 249, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.004 (0.4 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.012] (0 – 1.2 percentage points) from 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729). Repair outcomes: the single discordant pair was converted to pass by the single permitted automated repair (repair-conversion = 1/250). No preregistered exclusions, contamination flags, or missing pairs occurred. All numeric values are taken directly from archived analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; analysis/condition_summary.csv) and deterministic reconciliation manifests.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: the preregistered primary hypothesis (expecting ≥15 percentage-point sim-to-real paired deficit) is not supported in the executed confirmatory partition. Possible readings: (A) in tightly scoped, synthetic/emulation tasks with constrained intents and limited allowed fields, gpt-5-mini produced candidates that were already largely consistent with mechanistic validator encodings; (B) the validator and task generator encoded mechanically checkable properties for which modern LLMs perform well; or (C) the confirmatory partition and single-repair policy limited observable failure mass. Preregistration reconciliation and power: the preregistered power calculation assumed a baseline emulation pass rate ≈ 0.90 and targeted a 15-percentage-point effect; the observed baseline pass rate (0.996) is far higher than the assumption, so the run has low sensitivity to detect small paired differences (the observed 95% CI upper bound = 1.2 percentage points). Therefore the study is confirmatory for the shared_initial_candidate estimand as executed, but it was not powered to detect small effects around the observed high pass rate or to support the original sim-to-real contrast that would require execution of production-like partitions. Threats to validity: Internal — results depend on prompt templates, declared model, single repair policy, and the strict shared_initial_candidate design (which we explicitly state and enforce). Construct — the validator checks mechanically verifiable properties (syntax and prescribed workflow sequences); we did not evaluate broader semantic correctness (protocol dynamics, performance). External — confirmatory execution was limited to the synthetic/emulation partition; community and production-like partitions remain exploratory and unexecuted in this run. Security and adversarial limits: adaptive prompt-injection, retrieval-based attacks, vendor-specific CLI subtleties, and heterogeneous real production topologies were not exercised and remain open directions. Operational implication: in similarly constrained emulation-style tasks a guarded GVR pipeline may yield small marginal verifier gains because modern LLMs already produce largely validator-consistent candidates; do not generalize this conclusion beyond the studied regime.
sections.conclusion: We executed a sealed, preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics to measure the verifier-detected benefit of deterministic validation plus one automated repair on identical LLM-generated configuration candidates. In N=250 constrained synthetic intent tasks, initial gpt-5-mini candidates passed the deterministic validator in 249/250 cases and the guarded pipeline converted the single failing candidate; paired improvement = 0.4 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 1.2 pp], p = 1.0). The preregistered near-null result implies that GVR-style guardrails can produce limited marginal verifier benefit in some tightly constrained NetOps task regimes; broader, adversarial, and production-like settings require further, partition-specific study. All execution manifests, raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis artifacts are archived and hashed in the evidence bundle referenced by the preregistration manifest.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: the executed confirmatory run was limited to the synthetic/emulation partition described in the preregistration; the community and production-like partitions listed in the preregistration were not executed in the confirmatory run and remain exploratory.

Validator coverage: the deterministic validator checked mechanically verifiable properties (syntax, prescribed workflow sequences); broader semantic correctness (protocol dynamics, performance, emergent interactions) was not assessed.
Model and tooling scope: a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator implementation were used; results do not establish multi-model or alternate-validator generality.

Adversary and retrieval attacks: adaptive prompt-injection, retrieval-based attacks, vendor-targeted exploit vectors, and heterogeneous real-world topologies were not evaluated and remain open threats.
Repair policy: only one automated repair attempt was permitted by design; multi-iteration repair loops, human-in-the-loop escalation, or different repair templates may change outcomes.
